noteBlocks.md: Your pancreas makes insulin every time your blood glucose rises. Someone with type 1 diabetes cannot, so they inject it, and what they inject can be human insulin made by bacteria. Getting a bacterium to make a human protein takes one gene, two cuts, one join and a very large tank.

noteBlocks.md:
An organism's **genome** is all of its genetic material. **Genetic engineering** changes the genome to give the organism a **desirable characteristic** it did not have.

A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for one protein, and insulin is a protein. Move the human insulin gene into a bacterium, and the bacterium makes human insulin.

noteBlocks.md:
A **restriction enzyme** cuts DNA only where it finds one particular **base sequence**. Each enzyme has its own sequence, and a question always tells you which. The enzyme in this lesson looks for TCGA.

It cuts the top strand between T and C, and the bottom strand two bases further along. This **staggered cut** leaves a few unpaired bases hanging off each end: **sticky ends**.

noteBlocks.title: Why the ends are sticky
noteBlocks.md: The unpaired bases on one end are complementary to the unpaired bases on the other: C pairs with G and G with C. So any two ends this enzyme leaves can pair up again, like the two halves of a zip.

noteBlocks.explain: Sticky ends. Describing them as loose or matching is true, but the mark is for the name.

noteBlocks.md:
**Worked example.** Into how many sections is this length of DNA cut?
**Step 1: find every site.** Read the top strand from the left. TCGA appears at bases 3 to 6 and 11 to 14.
**Step 2: one site, one staggered cut.** The bottom strand under each site reads TCGA from right to left, so it is cut too, two bases along: 2 cuts.
**Step 3: count the sections.** A straight length already has two ends, so every cut adds a section: 2 + 1 = **3 sections**.

noteBlocks.prompt: The same enzyme cuts between T and C wherever the top strand reads TCGA. This top strand reads ACTCGATTGTCGACTTCGAG. Into how many sections is this length of DNA cut?
noteBlocks.explain: TCGA appears 3 times, at bases 3 to 6, 10 to 13 and 16 to 19, so there are 3 staggered cuts and 3 + 1 = 4 sections.

noteBlocks.md: A **plasmid** is a small ring of DNA in a bacterium, separate from its chromosome. The **same restriction enzyme** cuts the plasmid open. It cuts at the same base sequence, so the plasmid's sticky ends are **complementary** to the gene's. The gene pairs into the gap and is joined in. The ring that results is a **recombinant plasmid**.

noteBlocks.md: That is why one cut is enough for the plasmid: it opens the ring without breaking it into pieces. On a ring, n cuts give n pieces; on a straight length, n cuts give n + 1.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why is the plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme that cut out the insulin gene?
options: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
so the enzyme is used up
so the plasmid falls into many pieces
noteBlocks.answer: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
noteBlocks.explain: Same enzyme, same base sequence, complementary sticky ends. A different enzyme would leave ends that do not pair.

noteBlocks.text: 5. Into a bacterium, then a fermenter

noteBlocks.md:
The recombinant plasmid is put into a bacterium, which is now **genetically modified**. The modified bacteria are grown in a **fermenter**. There the bacteria **multiply**, their plasmids are copied each time, and every bacterium uses the human gene to make **human insulin**.

Insulin is a **protein**, so the bacterium builds it from **amino acids**, in the order the gene codes for.

noteBlocks.md: Summer 2024's report names this: answers saying the plasmid contained the hormone could not score. The plasmid carries the **insulin gene**. The insulin does not exist until the bacterium makes it.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the fermenter, what happens to the genetically modified bacteria and their plasmids?
options: they multiply
they are purified
they are cut open
noteBlocks.explain: They multiply, or reproduce. Purifying comes later, and the cutting was done before the plasmid went into the bacterium.

noteBlocks.md: At the end the fermenter holds a broth of bacteria, leftover food, waste and insulin. **Downstreaming** turns it into a medicine in three stages: **extraction** (take the insulin out), **purification** (remove everything that is not insulin) and **packaging**. It is needed so that a **pure** form of insulin, safe to inject, reaches the patient.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is an advantage of making insulin with genetically modified bacteria?
options: it is identical to human insulin
it needs no genes at all
it is made without any protein
noteBlocks.answer: it is identical to human insulin
noteBlocks.explain: Identical to human insulin. The other advantages are large quantities, lower cost, and no animal being used.

whyMenu.explain: TCGA is its own partner read backwards, so wherever the top strand has a site the bottom strand has one too, directly underneath. One sweep of the top strand finds every site.

steps.decision: The top-strand cut and the bottom-strand cut at one site are two halves of the same staggered cut. Count sites, not strand cuts.

Every cell has cytoplasm.
Bacteria do have DNA. What they lack is a nucleus to keep it in.

options.text: a section of DNA that codes for one protein
options.feedback: A section of DNA coding for one protein. The insulin gene codes for insulin.

A pairs with T.
T pairs with A.

options.text: it is a type of sugar
options.feedback: Enzymes are proteins.

items.stem: Which type of enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA?

Amylase breaks down starch and has nothing to do with DNA.

items.stem: What are the short single-stranded ends left by a staggered cut called?

options.feedback: Sticky ends. They pair with any end the same enzyme has cut, because their bases are complementary.

They do match, but the specification's name is sticky ends.
The name on the specification is sticky ends.

options.feedback: 6. Each site is one staggered cut, and a straight length gives one more section than it has cuts.
That is the number of cuts. A straight length already has two ends, so add one.
That counts each strand's cut separately. The two halves of a staggered cut are one cut.
That subtracts one instead of adding one. Every cut on a straight length adds a section.

items.stem: This enzyme cuts between T and C in TCGA. At one site it cuts the top strand in gap 3. Where is the bottom strand cut at that site?

options.feedback: Gap 5. The bottom strand, read right to left, is cut between its own T and C, two bases along: a staggered cut.

options.text: it is not cut at all

options.text: at the end of the whole molecule
options.feedback: The bottom strand is cut at the same site, just a little further along.

The bacterium supplies its own amino acids. The plasmid carries the gene that sets their order.

hints: Seven things happen, and each is one short sentence.

parts.workedSolution: A restriction enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA. Its staggered cut leaves sticky ends on the gene. A plasmid is taken from a bacterium and cut open with the same restriction enzyme, so its sticky ends are complementary to the gene's. The gene is joined into the plasmid, making a recombinant plasmid, and the plasmid is put into a bacterium, which is now a genetically modified bacterium. The modified bacteria multiply in a fermenter, and each one uses the human gene to make insulin. Finally, downstreaming: the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged, so that a pure form reaches the patient.

commonErrors.feedback: The plasmid carries the gene, not the hormone. Summer 2024 named this as the answer examiners could not credit: the insulin does not exist until the bacterium makes it.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara is given a length of DNA and told that a restriction enzyme cuts it wherever the top strand reads TCGA. She is asked how many sections it will be cut into. Her working:
studentWorking: TCGA appears 3 times on the top strand.
Each site is one staggered cut, so there are 3 cuts.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 gives the number of cuts as the number of sections. A straight length of DNA already has two ends, so every cut adds one more section: 3 cuts make 4 sections.
correction: TCGA appears 3 times on the top strand.
Each site is one staggered cut, so there are 3 cuts.
findTheMistake.feedback: The sites and the cuts were found correctly, and that is the harder half. Summer 2025 records that only the more able candidates gave the right number of sections here: counting cuts and forgetting the extra piece is exactly how the mark goes.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor is asked to describe three stages of making human insulin, one mark each. His answer:
studentWorking: The insulin gene is joined into a plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme.
The plasmid carries insulin into the bacterium.
The bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 3 are correct and well worded. Line 2 puts the hormone inside the plasmid. What the plasmid carries is the human insulin gene. No insulin exists until the bacterium makes it from that gene.
correction: The insulin gene is joined into a plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme.
The plasmid carries the human insulin gene into the bacterium.
The bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks stand. The report for Summer 2024 names this one: candidates wrote that the plasmid contained the hormone when the mark needed the gene. One word, gene, is the whole difference.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is asked what happens in the fermenter and what happens next, one mark each. Her answer:
studentWorking: The genetically modified bacteria are placed in a fermenter.
In the fermenter, the bacteria and their plasmids grow.
Afterwards the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 3 are right. Line 2 says the bacteria and plasmids grow, but the mark is for making more of them: they multiply, or reproduce. A few bacteria growing bigger would make very little insulin.
correction: The genetically modified bacteria are placed in a fermenter.
In the fermenter, the bacteria and their plasmids multiply.
Afterwards the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand. Summer 2024 accepted only reproduction or multiplication for this part, because the question was about the bacterium and its plasmid together. Grow is the word that cost the mark.

prompts.answer: Changing the genome of an organism to give it a desirable characteristic.

prompts.prompt: Name the type of enzyme that cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA, and name the ends it leaves.
prompts.answer: A restriction enzyme, and it leaves sticky ends.

prompts.prompt: Why is the same restriction enzyme used on the human DNA and on the plasmid?
prompts.answer: It cuts at the same base sequence both times, so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join the plasmid.

prompts.prompt: A restriction enzyme finds its site n times along a straight length of DNA. How many sections are made? And on a ring?
prompts.answer: A straight length gives n + 1 sections, because it already has two ends. A ring gives n pieces, because the first cut only opens it.

prompts.prompt: What makes a restriction enzyme's cut staggered?
prompts.answer: It cuts the two strands at different points, a few bases apart, which leaves single-stranded sticky ends.
A plasmid that has had a gene from another organism joined into it: here, the human insulin gene.

prompts.prompt: Does the plasmid carry insulin or the insulin gene into the bacterium?
prompts.answer: The insulin gene. The bacterium makes the insulin from it afterwards.

prompts.prompt: What happens to the modified bacteria and their plasmids in the fermenter?
prompts.answer: They multiply: the bacteria reproduce, the plasmids are copied, and each bacterium makes human insulin.

prompts.prompt: What are the three stages of downstreaming, and why is it needed?
prompts.answer: Extraction, purification and packaging. It is needed so that a pure form of insulin reaches the patient.

prompts.prompt: Give three advantages of making human insulin with genetically modified bacteria.
prompts.answer: It is identical to human insulin, it can be made in large quantities and cheaply, and no animal is used.
